questions.prompt: A parent state update queues a render. What normally happens to its un-memoized child?

choices.text: React waits for the browser to repaint before evaluating the child.
React replaces the child DOM subtree before calling its function.
React skips the child unless the child state also changed.
React calls the child while calculating the next output.

questions.explanation: Rendering recursively calls returned components. A child does not need its own state update to be evaluated.

sources.title: Render and Commit
sources.claim: React triggers rendering initially or after state updates, calls components to calculate output, commits necessary DOM changes and then the browser paints; rendering must be pure.

questions.prompt: Which operation queues another render after initial mounting?

choices.text: Assigning a new value to ref.current without setting state.
Assigning to an ordinary local variable in a component.
Calling the component state setter with a changed value.
Reading an existing DOM attribute without updating state.

questions.explanation: Calling the setter with changed state queues rendering. Local assignments, ref.current assignments and DOM reads do not notify React to render.

questions.prompt: A component increments a shared module counter during rendering. Why is this unsafe?

choices.text: Only mutations of DOM nodes can make a component impure.
A shared counter is safe whenever the return value is valid JSX.
React guarantees exactly one render call per DOM mutation.
Rendering must not mutate values that existed before that render.

questions.explanation: Rendering should be pure. Repeated or abandoned calculations must not accumulate external changes.

questions.prompt: Why may Strict Mode call a component twice during development?

choices.text: To guarantee two browser paints for every state change.
To expose bugs caused by impure rendering calculations.
To make every network request execute twice in production.
To apply each state replacement twice before committing.

questions.explanation: Development checks help find impurity. They do not promise doubled production updates or paints.

questions.prompt: A state update re-renders a clock whose JSX text is unchanged. What must the commit do?

choices.text: Replace every DOM node because component execution occurred.
Apply only necessary changes, potentially no DOM mutation.
Skip comparison and schedule a DOM mutation on the next event.
Rebuild the whole document before comparing old and new JSX.

questions.explanation: React compares the output and commits only necessary DOM changes. Render calls are not a count of mutations.

questions.prompt: Which ordering best describes a visible React update?

choices.text: Trigger, browser paint, calculate output, commit DOM changes.
Browser paint, calculate output, trigger, commit DOM changes.
Commit DOM changes, trigger, browser paint, calculate output.
Trigger, calculate output, commit DOM changes, browser paint.

questions.explanation: React calculates and commits; the browser then displays the changed pixels. React rendering is distinct from browser painting.

questions.prompt: Which events and steps belong to the React update process? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Every component call automatically replaces its DOM node.
An initial root render starts component evaluation.
Reading a local variable automatically queues an update.
A state change can queue component evaluation.
A parent update skips every child whose local state is unchanged.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: commit applies only necessary differences. B: Correct: initial rendering is a trigger. C: Incorrect: reads do not notify React. D: Correct: state setters can queue rendering. E: Incorrect: un-memoized returned child components are evaluated recursively.

questions.prompt: Which practices preserve render purity? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Return the same output for the same component inputs.
Send an analytics request every time the function evaluates.
Keep external synchronization outside render calculations.
Modify a pre-existing shared array while building the JSX.
Calculate JSX from the current props and state.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: deterministic inputs and output are a purity requirement. B: Incorrect: requests are externally observable side effects. C: Correct: rendering should mind its own calculation. D: Incorrect: shared mutation violates purity. E: Correct: rendering derives the description of the UI.

questions.prompt: Which claims about calculation and DOM commit are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Component execution alone proves a visible DOM change occurred.
React calculates differences before applying them to the DOM.
Commit applies the DOM changes necessary for the new output.
Every re-render requires destroying every existing DOM node.
Unchanged output can leave existing DOM nodes untouched.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: identical output can yield no changes. B: Correct: calculation precedes commit. C: Correct: commit makes the calculated output concrete. D: Incorrect: React preserves nodes where possible. E: Correct: rendering need not cause mutation.

questions.prompt: Which distinctions prevent confusing React rendering with browser painting? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Browser paint is the same operation as calling a component.
React rendering calls components to determine their output.
One component function call always corresponds to one separate browser paint.
Rendering means the browser has already drawn new pixels.
DOM changes are applied during the commit step.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: painting is a browser display operation. B: Correct: this is React rendering terminology. C: Incorrect: React calculation and browser painting are distinct operations. D: Incorrect: component calculation precedes visible painting. E: Correct: commit updates the host DOM.
